title: Solder Joint Fatigue and Creep Cracking
introduction: Solder joint fatigue and creep cracking is the structural failure of the soldered electrical interconnections between silicon cells in a PV module. Under cyclic thermo-mechanical stress from CTE mismatch during daily and seasonal temperature cycling, microcracks nucleate in the solder and grow incrementally with each cycle — a fatigue process. Simultaneously, elevated temperature phases drive time-dependent creep deformation in the solder alloy that further accumulates damage. As cracks grow they increase electrical resistance across the joint; if a crack propagates across the full joint cross-section, the interconnect opens and the electrical circuit is broken.
reasoning: The 1261-MDPI study links CTE-mismatch thermo-mechanical stress under field thermal cycling directly to microcrack development, creep damage accumulation, and eventual open-circuit failure in PV solder interconnects.

key_findings.claim: Fatigue microcracks develop in solder interconnections as a result of thermo-mechanical stress from cyclic temperature loading
key_findings.detail: The development of microcracks is one of the results of solder joint deterioration under cyclic thermo-mechanical loading from CTE mismatch. [^mdpi1261a] The initiation and development of fatigue cracks in the solder interconnection is directly caused by the variation in CTE of bonded module materials during cycling. [^mdpi1261b]

key_findings.claim: A solder crack spanning the entire joint cross-section produces an open circuit and increases electrical resistance
key_findings.detail: If a fatigue crack spreads across the entire solder joint region, the result is an open circuit. [^mdpi1261c] An open circuit increases the electrical resistance across the solder joint, which is linked to power loss through the relation I²Rs. [^mdpi1261d]
